findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. They could explain it to someone else after reading only this.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The second section on the page is an error message. It appears right where a newcomer expects proof of what the lede promises: a commit traced to the models, cost and verdict. This makes the tool look broken, and the page never shows that traceability.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: A newcomer who came to Athena's site gets a long technical study of a different project, firstmate. The lede explains why the study is here, but most of the page (states, transitions, 45 claims) is about firstmate, and an Athena newcomer is unlikely to read it.
findings.source: Title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and lede "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project..."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete: prerequisites, a clone command, `./setup.sh` and a first command, and the header links straight to them. This covers "what do I do next" well.
findings.source: Next steps: "git 2.40 or later; a C linker (cc)...; curl...; Claude Code, or npm to install it" and "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page does not say which models Athena uses, or whether a paid account or API key is needed. It also gives no idea of typical cost, though it stresses that cost is recorded. A newcomer can't judge what it takes to try Athena before installing it.
findings.source: Next steps: "Claude Code, or npm to install it"; lede: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it"

findings.text: This link speaks to the site owner, not to a visitor. A newcomer won't know what "proposals" or "your decision" mean here.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: This section and the footer describe the repository's internal layout. That means nothing to a first-time reader.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."

findings.text: The firstmate part is carefully written: terms are defined before they are used, and every statement links to a cited source line. A reader who wants to check Athena's claim of traceable explanations can do so.
